claims.text: In-situ high-resolution TEM/STEM coupled with EDS can directly map elemental redistribution during high-temperature oxidation.
Such in-situ TEM/STEM-EDS observations can elucidate the mechanistic role of nanoprecipitates in oxidation.
Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is a dual-nanoprecipitation high-entropy alloy.
The additively manufactured alloy has nanoscale precipitates in a refined microstructure.
TEM lamellae of the alloy will be oxidized at approximately 850–1050 °C in an in-situ heating stage.
Oxidation will be conducted in an oxygen-containing atmosphere or air while imaging and elemental mapping are performed continuously.
Nanoprecipitate composition and morphology may change during oxidation through interfacial reactions and elemental diffusion.
Oxidation causes selective diffusion and redistribution of elements at and around nanoprecipitates.
Ti or Cr may become enriched in protective oxide layers during oxidation.
High-resolution STEM-EDS can capture oxidation-induced elemental changes dynamically at the nanoscale.
The precipitation state influences the formation and stability of protective oxide scales.
Progressive segregation of Cr and Ti is expected at nanoprecipitate interfaces during oxidation.
The oxide-scale structure of the additively manufactured alloy is expected to differ from that of cast or wrought counterparts.
Elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitates should correlate with the alloy's additional strength.
Elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitates should correlate with improved oxidation resistance.
Cast and wrought equivalents typically have less-refined microstructures than the additively manufactured alloy.
Cast and wrought equivalents have nanoprecipitate distributions different from those of the additively manufactured alloy.
TEM observations are restricted to nanoscale regions and may not represent bulk oxidation behavior.
The TEM vacuum, gas-cell, or electron-beam environment may alter oxidation kinetics relative to service conditions.
Local microstructural variation and beam effects create uncertainty in quantitatively assessing segregation pathways and kinetics.
